author: Ibn Battuta
title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta, A.D. 1325 to 1354, vols. 1 to 4
publisher: Hakluyt Society (Cambridge University Press for vols. 1 to 3; Hakluyt Society, London, for vol. 4)
translator: H. A. R. Gibb (vols. 1 to 3); vol. 4 translation by Gibb, completed with notes by C. F. Beckingham
note: Egypt in 1326 is vol. 1, pp. 18 to 71; Mali in 1352 to 1353 is vol. 4, pp. 946 on. His account of Egypt is compiled from several visits. Use only what he says he saw.

author: Nehemia Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, eds.
title: Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History
note: 492 pp. Al-Umari on Mansa Musa in Cairo, pp. 269 to 273. The twelve years of cheap gold is al-Umari's claim alone; Schultz 2006 doubts it.

author: S. D. Goitein
title: Letters of Medieval Jewish Traders
note: xviii + 359 pp. Geniza letters; shows how merchants and agents worked, not events of the 1330s.

author: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti
title: La pratica della mercatura, ed. Allan Evans
note: liv + 443 pp. Edition of the Italian, no translation. A merchant's handbook; its lists guide, they do not record prices.

author: Robert S. Lopez and Irving W. Raymond
title: Medieval Trade in the Mediterranean World: Illustrative Documents
translator: Robert S. Lopez and Irving W. Raymond
note: xi + 458 pp. Records of Civilization, no. 52. Contracts, letters and manuals in translation.

author: Ibn Khaldun
title: The Muqaddimah: An Introduction to History
publisher: Pantheon Books (2nd ed. Princeton University Press, 1967)
note: His account of the plague of 1348 is in vol. 1, about p. 64. He writes decades after the plague and gives his own views on trade.

author: Ibn Jubayr
title: The Travels of Ibn Jubayr
note: 430 pp. Describes the Qus to Aydhab route 140 years before the game. Use for how the route worked, not for 1324 prices.

author: S. D. Goitein
title: A Mediterranean Society, vol. 1: Economic Foundations
note: xxvi + 550 pp. Geniza merchants' letters and contracts. Its picture of one free Mediterranean society has been qualified.

author: Abraham L. Udovitch
title: Partnership and Profit in Medieval Islam
period: legal texts of the 8th to 11th century
note: xii + 282 pp. The qirad and other partnerships from jurists' handbooks; shows the rules, not how often they were kept.

author: Janet L. Abu-Lughod
title: Before European Hegemony: The World System A.D. 1250 to 1350
note: 443 pp. Cairo is ch. 9. Use for the map of links, not for the cause of anything; her account of Egypt and of decline is criticised.

author: Eliyahu Ashtor
title: A Social and Economic History of the Near East in the Middle Ages
note: 384 pp. Also issued by the University of California Press. Rests on a Mamluk decline thesis that later historians dispute.

author: Eliyahu Ashtor
title: Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages
note: xxii + 599 pp. Price series from Venetian and Genoese records are the useful part; the decline thesis is disputed.

author: Frederic C. Lane
title: Venice: A Maritime Republic
note: xiii + 505 pp. Galley convoys; the papal bans on trade with Egypt and their licences.

author: David Abulafia
title: The Great Sea: A Human History of the Mediterranean
note: 783 pp. A general history for the teacher's frame, not a source for a card.

author: K. N. Chaudhuri
title: Trade and Civilisation in the Indian Ocean: An Economic History from the Rise of Islam to 1750
note: xiv + 269 pp. Monsoon timing and the Red Sea trade.

author: George F. Hourani
title: Arab Seafaring in the Indian Ocean in Ancient and Early Medieval Times
note: viii + 131 pp.; expanded edition by John Carswell, 1995, xvii + 189 pp. Sound on the basics of dhows and monsoons, old on the rest.

author: Robert Irwin
title: The Middle East in the Middle Ages: The Early Mamluk Sultanate, 1250 to 1382
note: 180 pp. The sultan al-Nasir Muhammad's reigns and the emirs.

author: Andre Raymond
title: Cairo
period: Cairo from its founding; Mamluk chapters
note: viii + 436 pp. Markets, wakalas, the size of the city. Translator named from MER-10; not seen in a catalogue record. Population figures are disputed.

author: Boaz Shoshan
title: Popular Culture in Medieval Cairo
note: xv + 148 pp. Festivals and everyday life.

author: Ira M. Lapidus
title: Muslim Cities in the Later Middle Ages
note: xiv + 307 pp. Old; some claims about Cairo were revised later.

author: Michael W. Dols
title: The Black Death in the Middle East
note: 408 pp. Alexandria in autumn 1347; Cairo struck in autumn 1348 as the secondary reports have it (pages unchecked). Death tolls are the chroniclers' and Dols says so.

author: Michael W. Dols
title: The Second Plague Pandemic and Its Recurrences in the Middle East: 1347 to 1894
publisher: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 22, no. 2, pp. 162 to 189 (Brill)
note: Later waves of plague.

author: Stuart J. Borsch
title: The Black Death in Egypt and England: A Comparative Study
note: xii + 195 pp. Argues Egypt's damage was larger and longer than England's because of how land was held; a note resting on this work alone says so.

author: Nehemia Levtzion
title: Ancient Ghana and Mali
note: x + 283 pp. Dates and the reach of Mali rest on few sources.

author: Timothy F. Garrard
title: Myth and Metrology: The Early Trans-Saharan Gold Trade
publisher: Journal of African History 23, no. 4, pp. 443 to 461 (Cambridge University Press)
note: How much gold moved and in what units; contested.

author: Peter Jackson
title: The Mongols and the Islamic World: From Conquest to Conversion
note: xxi + 614 pp. The Ilkhanate under Abu Said, who died at the end of 1335 without an heir; contested only on why it broke up.

author: Bernard Lewis
title: Race and Slavery in the Middle East: An Historical Enquiry
note: vii + 184 pp. For the About page only: that the trade ran on these routes is not disputed; Lewis's framing is.

author: Warren C. Schultz
title: Mansa Musa's Gold in Mamluk Cairo: A Reappraisal of a World Civilizations Anecdote
publisher: Harrassowitz (in History and Historiography of Post-Mongol Central Asia and the Middle East, eds. Pfeiffer and Quinn)
note: Not one of the 27; added by MER-20 and not yet read in full. Cairo's gold rate fell about 25:1 to 20:1 from 1324 and is one of several short swings; al-Umari alone says twelve years. Check pages on a library copy before a card cites it.
